summary: A set of measurements of how fast a TENEX host could send data over the ARPANET. The author wrote a simple program that sent strings to itself and counted throughput, then tabulated results for different byte sizes. It reports real baud rate and the share of CPU used.

eli5.summary: Someone tested how fast one computer can push data through the network and how hard it has to work, and wrote down the numbers.

subtitle: Measurement of TENEX host bandwidth over ARPANET

tldr.problem: It is unclear how much throughput TENEX hosts can achieve when sending data over ARPANET and how much CPU they need.
tldr.mechanism: A TENEX program sent strings to itself over the network in samples of a million bits, measuring both real baud rate and CPU bandwidth used under different configurations.
tldr.outcome: Real throughput varies from 22 kilobits per second to 61 kilobits per second depending on byte size and mode; CPU usage ranges from 15% to 99% of capacity depending on the transfer configuration.

today: RFC 415 documented TENEX performance characteristics measured in 1972. The data remains an early empirical study of network host throughput, though modern systems are vastly faster.

sections.title: Measuring Network Throughput
sections.content: This note measures how fast a TENEX host can send data over ARPANET and how much CPU effort it requires. The author wrote a simple program that sent strings to itself, using either buffered or unbuffered I/O modes, and measured the throughput with samples of a million bits.
sections.eli5: Someone tested how fast a computer could send data to itself across the network, counting both speed and effort.

sections.title: Buffered Mode Results
sections.content: Using buffered send mode with different byte sizes, real throughput ranges from 22 to 61 kilobits per second, with CPU usage from 15% to 40%. Larger byte sizes (400, 800 bytes) achieve better throughput (59-61 kilobits per second) using only 21-22% CPU. Smaller sizes (50-100 bytes) reach about 46-48 kilobits per second with 15-16% CPU. A larger configuration with 3200-byte blocks reaches 41.8 kilobits per second using 70% CPU.
sections.eli5: Sending in bigger chunks is faster but uses more CPU. Small chunks are slower and less demanding.

sections.title: Unbuffered Mode and System Limits
sections.content: Without buffered mode, throughput drops significantly: from 36 to 54 kilobits per second with 36-bit sizes, using 38-60% CPU, and from 12 to 20 kilobits per second with 8-bit sizes, using up to 99% CPU. For comparison, local TTYs and line printers achieve about 15-20 kilobytes CPU bandwidth. At 2400 baud, a single TTY uses 15% of the CPU. Three nested Telnet sessions almost saturate the compute capacity when outputting to a 2400-baud terminal. Network tape transmission via the TIP achieves about 7 kilobits per second, using about 30% CPU.
sections.eli5: Without buffering, the computer works much harder and goes slower. Local devices and nested network services can nearly use up all the CPU.
